cases.n: Royal Commission into Institutional Responses to Child Sexual Abuse — final report
cases.victims_note: 8,013 private sessions held May 2013–November 2017; more than 16,000 people contacted the Commission. Not a count of all victims.
cases.who: Religious, government and other institutions; evidence related to 3,489 institutions
cases.cover: Case studies documented destroyed or unkept records and the protection of institutional reputation over children, e.g. the Catholic Diocese of Ballarat ('records were deliberately not made or kept or were destroyed').
cases.d: The Royal Commission, announced in November 2012, delivered its final report on 15 December 2017 with a total of 409 recommendations across its reports. It held 8,013 private sessions, received 1,344 written accounts and heard evidence relating to 3,489 institutions. 58.1% of survivors in private sessions reported abuse in a religious institution, 32.5% in a government-run institution and 10.5% in other non-government institutions. The average age at first abuse was 10.4 years. Its recommendations led to the National Redress Scheme, which began on 1 July 2018.
cases.cite: Royal Commission final report, 15 December 2017, as summarised by knowmore legal service and by The Guardian (republished by BishopAccountability)

cases.n: Parramatta Training School for Girls and Hay Institution — Royal Commission Case Study 7
cases.place: Parramatta, New South Wales (and Hay, NSW)
cases.victims_note: Sixteen women gave statements to the 2014 public hearing; the home held thousands of girls between 1887 and 1974.
cases.who: NSW state child-welfare department; Parramatta Girls Home (Parramatta Training School for Girls), Hay Institution for Girls
cases.cover: Most alleged perpetrators were never reported or investigated; some resigned or were dismissed after inquiries; no criminal charges were laid.
cases.d: Parramatta Girls Home was a NSW state-run institution for girls from 1887 to 1974, many of them Aboriginal girls of the Stolen Generations. The Royal Commission's February 2014 hearing (Case Study 7, report October 2014) heard evidence about 11 men, most of them superintendents or deputies, accused of physical and sexual abuse. Most alleged perpetrators were never reported or investigated and no criminal charges were laid. A 2004 Senate inquiry had earlier taken statements from 20 former residents.
cases.cite: Royal Commission into Institutional Responses to Child Sexual Abuse, Report of Case Study No. 7, October 2014 (via Wikipedia)

cases.n: Bringing Them Home — Stolen Generations inquiry
cases.victims_note: 535 Aboriginal people gave testimony; more than 600 further submissions. The report said that in certain regions and periods the share of Indigenous children forcibly removed was 'undoubtedly much greater than one in ten'.
cases.who: Commonwealth, state and territory governments; church and state institutions, foster and adoptive families
cases.cover: The report documented officials misrepresenting capable parents as unfit and telling some parents their children had died when they had not.
cases.d: The Human Rights and Equal Opportunity Commission inquiry, led by Sir Ronald Wilson and Mick Dodson, began in May 1995 and released 'Bringing Them Home' in April 1997. Among 502 inquiry witnesses, 17% of women and 7.7% of men reported sexual assault while in an institution, at work, or in a foster or adoptive family. It found institutions had severe discipline, child labour, poor food and physical and emotional abuse. Prime Minister Kevin Rudd delivered a national apology on 13 February 2008.
cases.cite: Human Rights and Equal Opportunity Commission, Bringing Them Home, April 1997 (via Wikipedia 'Stolen Generations', citing the report)

cases.n: Forde Inquiry — abuse of children in Queensland institutions
cases.who: 159 government and non-government orphanages, reformatories and detention centres in Queensland
cases.d: The Commission of Inquiry into Abuse of Children in Queensland Institutions, chaired by former governor Leneen Forde, was set up on 13 August 1998 and reported in May 1999. It examined 159 institutions from 1911 to 1999, found that abuse had occurred and made 42 recommendations. Some findings were sealed because matters were still before the courts. It led to state apologies, the Queensland Government Redress Scheme and the Forde Foundation.
cases.cite: Commission of Inquiry into Abuse of Children in Queensland Institutions (Forde Inquiry), May 1999 (via Wikipedia and Qld Government)

cases.n: Mullighan Inquiry — Children in State Care, South Australia
cases.who: South Australian state guardianship system (Families SA and predecessors)
cases.d: Commissioner Ted Mullighan's inquiry began in November 2004 and was widened in 2007 to children on the Anangu Pitjantjatjara Yankunytjatjara (APY) Lands. Its March 2008 report found 'that in the past 65 years the State has failed to protect some of the children in its care from sexual abuse' and that record-keeping on 924 children who died in state care was manifestly inadequate. It made 54 recommendations, and 400 suspected abusers were reported to South Australia Police.
cases.cite: Children in State Care Commission of Inquiry (Mullighan Report), March 2008 (via Wikipedia)

cases.n: Royal Commission into the Protection and Detention of Children in the Northern Territory (Don Dale)
cases.place: Don Dale Youth Detention Centre, Berrimah, Darwin, NT
cases.who: Northern Territory Government youth detention and child protection systems
cases.cover: A 2014 media release falsely said six boys had escaped when CCTV showed one; two earlier reports (January 2015 review and the August 2015 Children's Commissioner report) were not acted on.
cases.d: After ABC Four Corners' 'Australia's Shame' aired on 25 July 2016 showing boys at Don Dale assaulted, stripped and tear-gassed, and a boy hooded and shackled in a restraint chair, a Royal Commission was set up on 28 July 2016. Its report, tabled on 17 November 2017, made 142 findings and 226 recommendations, including closing Don Dale. The High Court ruled in June 2020 that the 2014 tear-gassing was unlawful. The Corrections Minister was sacked the morning after the broadcast.
cases.cite: Royal Commission into the Protection and Detention of Children in the Northern Territory, final report, 17 November 2017 (via Wikipedia)

cases.n: Scouts Australia — Royal Commission and convictions
cases.who: Scouts Australia (NSW branch, Scouts Victoria)
cases.cover: A 14-page 1981 report by a senior Scout leader detailing allegations against NSW Branch Commissioner Roderick Corrie was not properly investigated or referred to police; Scouts Australia's head apologised in 2000.
cases.d: Former NSW Branch Commissioner Roderick Corrie was jailed for seven years in February 2000 after pleading guilty to eight of 77 charges of sexually abusing children as young as 11 between 1969 and 1995. A 1981 internal report on his abuse of four boys had not been referred to police. Other Scout leaders were convicted in Victoria, including Neville Budge in 2017 for abusing eight boys between 1995 and 2002. Scouts Australia was called before the Royal Commission over its handling of complaints.
cases.cite: Sydney Morning Herald reporting (2000) and Victorian court reports, via Wikipedia 'Scouts Australia'

cases.n: Scouting Ireland — 'Historical Sexual Abuse in Scouting: A Learning Review' (Elliott)
cases.place: Ireland (Larch Hill, Co. Dublin national office)
cases.victims_note: 275 known or suspected perpetrators across the two predecessor associations; by November 2018 108 alleged victims had been identified and records review was ongoing.
cases.who: Catholic Boy Scouts of Ireland (CBSI) and Scout Association of Ireland (SAI), merged as Scouting Ireland in 2004
cases.cover: The review found 'coverup and a failure to report abuse'; records were lost or destroyed; adults with a sexual interest in young people rose to positions of influence and prevented known offenders being removed.
cases.d: Safeguarding expert Ian Elliott's learning review, published by Scouting Ireland in May 2020, identified at least 275 known or suspected sex offenders in CBSI and SAI, mainly from the 1960s to the 1990s. It found a culture 'driven by self-interest', cronyism, and cover-up. Scouting Ireland accepted the findings and apologised; allegations against living people were passed to the Gardaí and Tusla.
cases.cite: Ian Elliott, 'Historical Sexual Abuse in Scouting: A Learning Review', published May 2020; RTÉ News 14 May 2020 (via Wikipedia)

cases.n: Lake Alice Hospital Child and Adolescent Unit — torture finding
cases.victims_note: NZ$10.7 million paid to 183 former patients after a 2001 apology; police interviewed 63 former patients.
cases.who: Lake Alice state psychiatric hospital, child and adolescent unit; psychiatrist Selwyn Leeks
cases.cover: The Crown's internal policy refused to recognise the long-term effects of abuse, forcing complaints to the UN Committee Against Torture in 2019.
cases.d: Children in the unit in the 1970s were given electric shocks without anaesthetic and paraldehyde injections as punishment; survivors also reported sexual abuse. The government apologised in 2001 and paid NZ$10.7 million to 183 former patients. Survivors took complaints to the UN Committee Against Torture in 2019. Police announced charges in 2021; psychiatrist Selwyn Leeks was found unfit to stand trial and died in January 2022. In December 2024 the government set redress of at least NZ$150,000 per survivor after the Royal Commission's Lake Alice findings.
cases.cite: Royal Commission of Inquiry into Abuse in Care, Lake Alice hearing (June 2021); RNZ 18 December 2024; NZ Police release 2021 (via Wikipedia)

cases.n: Muzaffarpur shelter home — TISS audit and convictions
cases.victims_note: Medical tests confirmed sexual abuse of 34 of 42 girls aged 7–17.
cases.who: Sewa Sankalp Evam Vikas Samiti (state-funded NGO run by Brajesh Thakur); Bihar Social Welfare Department
cases.cover: The then district child protection officer was among the accused; Bihar Social Welfare Minister Manju Verma resigned over the case; the Supreme Court criticised the state for funding the NGO and moved the trial to Delhi. CBI cleared Verma and her husband, a finding disputed by The Caravan.
cases.d: A social audit of Bihar shelter homes by the Tata Institute of Social Sciences, submitted in April 2018, flagged sexual abuse at the Muzaffarpur girls' home; an FIR followed on 31 May 2018. Medical examination confirmed sexual abuse of 34 of the 42 girls. The Supreme Court took suo motu cognizance on 2 August 2018 and moved the case to a Delhi POCSO court, which in January 2020 convicted Brajesh Thakur and 18 others; Thakur was sentenced to life imprisonment.
cases.cite: Tata Institute of Social Sciences audit (2018); Saket POCSO court judgment, January 2020; Firstpost, The Hindu, Indian Express (via Wikipedia)

cases.n: Royal Commission of Inquiry into Abuse in Care — 'Whanaketia' final report
cases.victims_note: Estimate: of about 655,000 children, young people and adults in state and faith-based care 1950–2019, about 200,000 were abused and more were neglected.
cases.who: State social welfare, disability, mental health, education, law-enforcement and faith-based care settings
cases.cover: Commissioners found the state failed to respond to signs of systemic abuse and neglect, and that by 2024 there had been very little progress on the redress system they recommended in 2021.
cases.d: The final report, made public on 24 July 2024, found abuse was rife in state and faith-based care and that sexual abuse was commonplace, with abusers grooming people in care. It estimated 200,000 of about 655,000 people in care between 1950 and 2019 were abused; Māori were more likely to be abused. Commissioners Coral Shaw, Andrew Erueti and Paul Gibson made 138 recommendations, including a specialist investigation unit and an independent Care Safe Agency, and called it 'a national disgrace'.
cases.cite: Royal Commission of Inquiry into Abuse in Care, 'Whanaketia', final report, 24 July 2024; RNZ, 24 July 2024

cases.n: Tasmanian Commission of Inquiry — Ashley Youth Detention Centre, Launceston General Hospital, schools and out-of-home care
cases.place: Tasmania (Ashley Youth Detention Centre, Deloraine; Launceston General Hospital)
cases.who: Tasmanian Government: Ashley Youth Detention Centre, Launceston General Hospital paediatric ward, public schools, Child Safety Services, Tasmania Police
cases.cover: Launceston General Hospital failed to act on a 2011 or 2012 disclosure about nurse James Griffin, leaving children at risk for eight years; Tasmania Police failed to act on 'highly probative' evidence from the Australian Federal Police in 2015; the government had been on notice about unlawful isolation at Ashley since at least 2013.
cases.d: The commission, called in 2020 after a podcast aired allegations against Launceston General Hospital paediatric nurse James Griffin (who died in 2019 after being charged with child sexual offences), released a 3,500-page final report in 2023 with 75 findings and 191 recommendations. It found the state's response to child sexual abuse since 2000 had too often been inadequate, sometimes to protect reputations. Children at Ashley Youth Detention Centre had experienced systematic harm and abuse for decades and sexual abuse remained a 'live and current' risk; the commission repeated its call for Ashley to close. Premier Jeremy Rockliff apologised in parliament.
cases.cite: Commission of Inquiry into the Tasmanian Government's Responses to Child Sexual Abuse in Institutional Settings, final report, 2023; AAP

cases.n: Hogar Seguro Virgen de la Asunción — abuse, trafficking alerts and fire killing 41 girls
cases.victims_note: 41 girls aged 14–17 died in the 8 March 2017 fire; the Human Rights Ombudsman had received 45 abuse reports 2012–2016.
cases.who: State-run children's home under the Secretariat of Social Welfare (SBS); National Civil Police
cases.cover: Officials ignored repeated complaints: in November 2016 the Human Rights Ombudsman asked the Inter-American Commission on Human Rights for precautionary measures citing mistreatment and a trafficking network recruiting children from the home. On the day of the fire police guarding the locked room did not let the girls out.
cases.d: The state home, built for 350–500, held 700–800 children in 2017. A contractor was convicted in 2014 of raping a disabled 17-year-old resident and two teachers were arrested for sexual assault. After a protest and escape on 7 March 2017, 51 girls were locked in a schoolroom; a fire broke out the next morning and 41 died. The Secretary of Social Welfare, his deputy and the home's director were arrested on 13 March 2017; on 12 August 2025 former secretary Carlos Rodas and five other officials were convicted of manslaughter and abuse of authority and sentenced to up to 25 years.
cases.cite: Guatemala Human Rights Ombudsman (PDH) request to IACHR, Nov 2016; IACHR press release 031/2017; Guatemalan court verdict 12 August 2025 (via Wikipedia)

cases.n: Casitas del Sur — children missing from church-run shelters
cases.place: Mexico City (also CAIFAC, Monterrey; 'La Casita', Cancún)
cases.victims_note: 126 children removed from the shelter in January 2009; as of March 2012, 14 children remained missing.
cases.who: Iglesia Cristiana Restaurada (Restored Christian Church) shelters; Mexico City Attorney General's Office (PGJDF), which placed children there
cases.cover: A Mexico City legislator accused officials of the District Attorney's office of negligence and complicity, saying they warned the shelter of searches so children could be moved.
cases.d: Children placed by Mexico City prosecutors in the private Casitas del Sur shelter went missing; in October 2008 officials were refused entry when trying to recover a girl whose release a judge had ordered. On 29 January 2009 police and human rights staff removed 126 children; seven staff were charged with obstruction of justice. The missing children were alleged to have been taken for illegal adoption or trafficking, and the federal Attorney General offered a reward for information.
cases.cite: Mexican federal Attorney General reward notice; UN Human Rights Council doc A/HRC/14/32/Add.1; CNN México 2012 (via Wikipedia)

cases.n: La Gran Familia ('Mamá Rosa') shelter raid, Zamora
cases.victims_note: 432 children (174 girls, 278 boys) and 138 adults freed on 15 July 2014.
cases.who: La Gran Familia shelter, founded 1947 by Rosa del Carmen Verduzco ('Mamá Rosa')
cases.cover: More than 40 complaints from parents had been filed with Michoacán's DIF and the federal Attorney General's Office (PGR) before the raid.
cases.d: On 15 July 2014 the PGR's organised-crime unit (SEIDO) raided the shelter and freed 432 children and 138 adults living in squalid conditions; the PGR said some had suffered sexual abuse, and residents reported rape, being held for years, food deprivation and forced begging. The PGR ruled out charging the 79-year-old founder because of age and mental decline; six others faced charges from unlawful imprisonment to organised crime. The PGR also investigated claims that the shelter in effect bought children through notarised parental waivers. Verduzco died in 2018.
cases.cite: Justice in Mexico (University of San Diego), 27 July 2014; Expansión, 3 June 2018

cases.n: SENAME — deaths and abuse in Chilean state child protection
cases.place: Chile (incl. Centro Galvarino, Estación Central, Santiago)
cases.victims_note: SENAME reported 1,313 children, adolescents and adults died 2005–mid-2016 across its protection and juvenile justice programmes; the UN Committee counted 210 deaths in residences 2005–2016 and found 6.8% of children in centres had been sexually abused in the past year.
cases.who: Servicio Nacional de Menores (SENAME), Ministry of Justice, and accredited private residences
cases.d: The death of an 11-year-old girl at SENAME's Galvarino centre in Santiago in April 2016 exposed conditions in the system; in October 2016 SENAME disclosed 1,313 deaths of people in its programmes between 2005 and mid-2016. In a report released on 30 July 2018 the UN Committee on the Rights of the Child found the Chilean state responsible for 'grave violations' of the Convention, including sexual abuse, torture and cruel treatment in SENAME residences over 40 years, overcrowding of up to 60% and 210 deaths in residences 2005–2016. A former national director was questioned as a suspect over children's deaths in 2018.
cases.cite: UN Committee on the Rights of the Child, inquiry under the Optional Protocol (report released 30 July 2018), via BioBioChile; SENAME figures October 2016 (via Spanish Wikipedia)

cases.n: Élan School, Poland, Maine — troubled-teen programme
cases.who: Élan School (private behaviour-modification boarding school; NATSAP member)
cases.cover: In the late 1970s staff refused a sheriff's lieutenant entry past the lobby after rumours of abuse.
cases.d: Élan operated from 1970 until 1 April 2011, when it closed after decades of abuse reports from former students. Illinois officials removed eleven children in 1975 alleging mistreatment, and in 2007 New York education officials, who paid tuition for special-education students, alleged students were made to restrain peers and were sleep-deprived. The New Yorker (2000) and Time (2011) described 'the ring', in which students were made to fight one another. Maine State Police reopened the 1982 death of a 15-year-old student in 2016 but filed no charges. The record of sexual abuse rests on former students' accounts; no official sexual-abuse finding was located.
cases.cite: New Yorker (2000); Time (2011); Lewiston Sun Journal; Maine State Police 2016 (via Wikipedia)

cases.n: Provo Canyon School, Utah — licences revoked 2026
cases.who: Provo Canyon School, owned by Universal Health Services (2000–2026)
cases.d: Provo Canyon School, a for-profit residential treatment centre owned by Universal Health Services, faced public accounts from former students including Paris Hilton (2020) of physical abuse, forced medication, strip-searches and seclusion. In June 2026 Utah's Department of Health and Human Services found staff failed to protect a resident during an assault and delayed medical treatment, and on 17 July 2026 revoked the licences of both campuses; UHS appealed. No official sexual-abuse finding was located; the licence revocation concerned failure to protect and safety.
cases.cite: Utah Department of Health and Human Services licence action, June–July 2026; Salt Lake Tribune, 27 July 2026 (via Wikipedia)

cases.n: Romanian state orphanages under Ceaușescu and after 1989
cases.place: Romania (incl. Siret children's psychiatric hospital; Sighetu Marmației institution)
cases.victims_note: About 100,000–170,000 children were in orphanages in 1989; an estimated 500,000 were raised in them overall.
cases.who: Romanian state orphanages and institutions for disabled children
cases.d: Decree 770 (1966) banned abortion, and many children born afterwards were abandoned in state institutions, where they suffered neglect, physical and sexual abuse and sedation; physical and sexual abuse was reported to be common at the Siret children's psychiatric hospital. After 1989 large numbers of children were adopted abroad amid corruption and irregularities, and in 2004, under EU pressure, Romania banned international adoption except by grandparents. A 2009 BBC investigation found poor conditions persisted in some institutions.
cases.cite: Wikipedia 'Romanian orphans' (citing BBC 2009 and academic sources)

cases.n: Nepal child care homes — 'paper orphans' and recruitment by agents
cases.place: Kathmandu Valley (Bagmati Province); children from Karnali and other rural districts
cases.victims_note: 10,905 children were in 417 registered child care homes in 2021/22 (National Child Rights Council); UNICEF says about 85% have at least one living parent or guardian.
cases.who: Child care homes (orphanages) in Nepal, many registered as NGOs; recruiting agents
cases.d: Nepal's National Child Rights Council counted 417 registered child care homes holding 10,905 children in 2021/22, and UNICEF estimates about 85% have a living parent or guardian. Agents take money from rural families with promises of schooling and are paid commissions by institutions; NGOs documented a child admitted on a forged parental death certificate. Researchers say homes use children to attract donations and that many operate unregistered. Only about 200 of 753 local governments had appointed the child welfare officers required by the Act Relating to Children (2018).
cases.cite: National Child Rights Council (NCRC) report 2021/22 and UNICEF, via The Annapurna Express

cases.n: Scouts Canada — KPMG review of unreported abuse
cases.victims_note: KPMG reviewed 468 files of suspected sexual misconduct over 64 years and found at least 65 incidents not reported to authorities.
cases.who: Scouts Canada
cases.cover: A 2011 CBC investigation found Scouts Canada had signed confidentiality agreements with more than a dozen abuse victims; KPMG found abusers had in some cases been 'removed discreetly' and records were inconsistent and poorly kept.
cases.d: After a CBC investigation in autumn 2011 found confidentiality agreements that kept victims from speaking, Scouts Canada apologised and asked KPMG to audit 64 years of records. The review, released in 2012, examined 468 files and found the organisation failed at least 65 times to report sexual misconduct allegations to authorities, 13 of them after 1992 when reporting became mandatory. Scouts Canada then gave police all records it could find. In 1979 the Boy Scouts of America had sent a known abuser back to Canada without warning Scouts Canada; he was convicted in Victoria, BC in 1996 of assaulting four boys.
cases.cite: KPMG review of Scouts Canada records, 2012, via Global News; CBC 2011 (via Wikipedia 'Scouting sex abuse cases')

cases.n: The Scout Association (UK) — abuse claims and payouts
cases.victims_note: At least 260 claims taken on by eight law firms in a decade; more than £6m paid across 166 settled cases (BBC File on 4, 2023).
cases.who: The Scout Association (UK)
cases.d: A BBC File on 4 investigation in June 2023 found, from data from eight specialist law firms, that at least 260 child sexual abuse claims had been taken on against the Scouts in the previous decade and more than £6m paid out across 166 settled cases. The Scouts said 96% of claims highlighted by a survivors' campaign related to offences before 2013 and that the payouts broadly matched what it knew. In 2014 the BBC had reported more than 50 historical claims and £897,000 in damages; an MP called for an inquiry into failures to pass abuse records to police.
cases.cite: BBC File on 4, June 2023, via Civil Society; BBC 2014 (via Wikipedia)

cases.n: Verband Christlicher Pfadfinder (VCP) — independent study of sexualised violence
cases.victims_note: At least 344 victims since 1973; at least 161 people committed or were accused of sexualised violence.
cases.who: Verband Christlicher Pfadfinderinnen und Pfadfinder (VCP), Protestant scouting federation
cases.cover: The study found 'old cases' from the 1980s and 1990s were long ignored for lack of any idea of reappraisal (Aufarbeitung).
cases.d: A study by the Munich Institut für Praxisforschung und Projektberatung (IPP) and the Dissens Institute, presented in Kassel on 27 January 2026, found at least 344 people had suffered sexualised violence within the VCP since 1973. It drew on 79 interviews and about 1,300 pages of files on 100 cases. About 60% of victims were girls, two-thirds were aged 13–17 when it began, nearly half the acts occurred after 2000, and more than half on camps or trips. Perpetrators came mostly from within the organisation, often adult group leaders.
cases.cite: IPP München and Dissens-Institut, VCP Aufarbeitungsstudie, 27 January 2026, via evangelisch.de

cases.n: Flanders — historical abuse in youth institutions and boarding schools, parliamentary apology
cases.who: Flemish youth institutions, youth centres and boarding schools
cases.d: After clergy abuse cases, further cases emerged of child abuse in Flemish institutions between 1930 and 1990. A working group of experts led by child psychiatrist Peter Adriaenssens, set up by Welfare Minister Jo Vandeurzen, produced two reports recognising the wide scope of abuse. On 23 April 2014 Flemish Parliament Speaker Jan Peumans formally apologised to victims of abuse in boarding schools and youth centres. A temporary recognition and mediation commission set up in 2014 was later made permanent; it received 121 reports in 2024.
cases.cite: VRT NWS, 23 April 2014; Belga News Agency, 23 February 2025

cases.n: Moldova — children leaving residential institutions targeted by traffickers
cases.victims_note: More than 14,000 children lived in residential care, over 70% of them 'social orphans' with living parents (UNICEF 2006). UNICEF said children in institutions were 'several times' (elsewhere '10 times') more vulnerable to trafficking than other children.
cases.who: Moldovan state residential institutions and boarding schools (Ministry of Education, Health, Labour)
cases.d: Moldova had 68 residential institutions for children in the mid-2000s; children left them at 15–16 with no support beyond about US$70 and no follow-up. UNICEF reported that research showed institutionalised children were several times more vulnerable to trafficking than other children and that 'they often become easy prey for traffickers'. The US State Department's March 2007 human rights report said women and children were trafficked for sexual exploitation to Russia, Turkey, Israel, the UAE and other countries, and that 12% of trafficking victims assisted by IOM were minors.
cases.cite: UNICEF (2005, 2006) and US State Department Country Report on Human Rights Practices 2006 (March 2007), compiled by ACCORD (Austrian Centre for Country of Origin and Asylum Research), query a-5839

cases.n: Ukraine orphanages as a 'recruitment tool' for traffickers — Disability Rights International 'No Way Home'
cases.place: Ukraine (33 institutions visited, incl. Vinnytsia oblast)
cases.victims_note: UNICEF estimated at least 82,000 children in Ukraine's residential institutions; DRI put the number near 100,000.
cases.who: Ukrainian state orphanages, boarding schools and institutions for children with disabilities
cases.d: Disability Rights International investigated 33 institutions between 2012 and 2015 and published 'No Way Home' in 2015. La Strada Ukraine told DRI that recruiting children from orphanages into prostitution is 'the most typical scheme' and that sexual exploitation in institutions typically begins around age 13, often instigated by staff; an IOM counter-trafficking coordinator called orphanages a direct feeder to domestic and international trafficking and said most documented cases originate in the vocational schools that orphanage leavers attend. DRI concluded that the orphanage system serves as a recruitment tool for traffickers.
cases.cite: Disability Rights International, 'No Way Home: The Exploitation and Abuse of Children in Ukraine's Orphanages', 2015 (citing La Strada Ukraine, IOM Ukraine, UNICEF, US State Department TIP 2014)

cases.n: Haiti — orphanage assessment identifies 3,019 potential trafficking victims
cases.victims_note: Potential trafficking victims identified in institutions by Haiti's social welfare agency IBESR.
cases.who: Private orphanages in Haiti; Institut du Bien-Être Social et de Recherches (IBESR)
cases.d: The US State Department's 2019 Trafficking in Persons Report states that Haiti's social welfare agency IBESR, 'after completing an assessment of more than 750 orphanages with another government and international NGOs, identified 3,019 potential victims of trafficking in those institutions'. IBESR closed eight non-compliant orphanages in the reporting period and expanded foster care to 121 accredited families to reduce children's vulnerability to trafficking.
cases.cite: US Department of State, Trafficking in Persons Report 2019 (Haiti), as quoted by Better Care Network

cases.n: Cambodia — orphanages buying children to attract donations
cases.place: Cambodia (incl. Siem Reap and Phnom Penh)
cases.who: Private residential care institutions ('orphanages') in Cambodia
cases.cover: The report states 'endemic corruption aids and abets trafficking crimes'.
cases.d: The US State Department's 2019 Trafficking in Persons Report states: 'Some Cambodian orphanages purchase local children from economically disadvantaged families and subject them to malnutrition and unclean living conditions in their facilities for the purpose of attracting and profiting from charitable donations; some of these children are at further risk of sex trafficking and domestic servitude as a result of poor government oversight of adoption processes.' The same report links orphanages and trafficking in Nepal, Nigeria, Haiti, Sri Lanka and Moldova.
cases.cite: US Department of State, Trafficking in Persons Report 2019 (Cambodia), as quoted by Better Care Network

cases.n: 'Hidden in Plain Sight' — Australian Parliament recognises orphanage trafficking as modern slavery
cases.place: Canberra (Joint Standing Committee on Foreign Affairs, Defence and Trade)
cases.who: Australian volunteers, donors, schools and tour operators supporting overseas orphanages
cases.d: The Joint Standing Committee's report 'Hidden in Plain Sight', released on 6 December 2017 from its inquiry into establishing a Modern Slavery Act, recognised orphanage trafficking as a form of modern slavery to be covered by the Act. A chapter was devoted to orphanage trafficking, orphanage tourism and Australian donations, with evidence from ReThink Orphanages, Lumos, the ChildSafe campaign and others. Australia's Modern Slavery Act followed in 2018; Lumos supported the change.
cases.cite: Parliament of Australia, Joint Standing Committee on Foreign Affairs, Defence and Trade, 'Hidden in Plain Sight', December 2017 (via Better Care Network)

cases.n: Deoria shelter home, Uttar Pradesh — girls rescued, CBI case
cases.victims_note: 24 girls rescued on 5 August 2018 from a home registering 42 inmates; 18 were missing.
cases.who: Maa Vindhyavasini Mahila Prashikshan Evam Samaj Sewa Sansthan (NGO); director Girija Tripathi and superintendent Kanchan Lata Tripathi
cases.cover: The UP Women and Child Development Minister said the NGO's recognition had been revoked and funds stopped a year earlier, yet it continued to operate; the government said it would examine who was responsible.
cases.d: The case came to light when a 10-year-old girl escaped to a women's police station and said girls were taken away in cars in the afternoons and returned crying in the morning. Police rescued 24 girls on 5 August 2018 and sealed the home. Police charge-sheeted the director and her daughter, and seven others in a second FIR. In 2019 the CBI took over and registered cases including sexual harassment, human trafficking, sexual assault and adoption without legal procedure.
cases.cite: PTI, 6 August 2018 (via Morung Express); PTI/CBI, 2019 (via ACT database)

cases.n: Dow Family Children's Home, Kenya — US conviction of founder
cases.place: Boito, rural area west of Nairobi, Kenya
cases.who: Dow Family Children's Home, founded 2008 by US missionary Gregory Dow
cases.d: Gregory Dow, from Lancaster County, Pennsylvania, opened an orphanage in Kenya in 2008 and sexually abused four girls aged 11 to 13 when the abuse began, between October 2013 and September 2017. He fled to the US after Kenyan authorities issued an arrest warrant; the home closed in September 2017. He was arrested in July 2019 and in June 2020 pleaded guilty in federal court in Philadelphia to four counts of illicit sexual conduct in a foreign place.
cases.cite: US Attorney's Office, Eastern District of Pennsylvania, July 2019 and June 2020 (via CNN and Diplomatic Times)

cases.n: Nyumbani Children's Home, Nairobi — USAID found abuse claims credible
cases.victims_note: Six former residents told the Washington Post they were sexually abused 2002–2018; a USAID investigation identified other cases.
cases.who: Nyumbani Children's Home for HIV-positive children, run by Children Of God Relief Institute (COGRI), a Catholic charity
cases.cover: A USAID memo (21 July 2022) said the co-founder had known of abuse allegations since 2006, 'neglected to document violence against children', permitted victim-blaming and 'systematically failed to respond to widespread sexual misconduct'; some survivors were made to write letters of apology.
cases.d: Nyumbani, opened in 1992, was among Africa's first homes for HIV-positive children and attracted large US donations. After a whistleblower complaint, a 2021 USAID investigation found abuse claims 'credible', including rape of children by volunteers, caregivers and other children. The Washington Post reported the findings on 27 November 2023 from court documents filed by the orphanage's Kenyan board. The co-founder stepped down after the Post's questions.
cases.cite: USAID investigation (2021) and memo of 21 July 2022, filed in Kenyan court, as reported by The Washington Post, 27 November 2023 (republished by BishopAccountability)

cases.n: Lechaina Children's Care Centre, Greece — caged beds and sedation
cases.who: State Children Care Center of Lechaina (children with disabilities)
cases.d: In March 2011 the Greek Ombudsman's Office published a report on the state care centre at Lechaina finding too few doctors and nurses, systematic sedation, residents tied to their beds and the use of wooden cage beds because of staff shortages; most children received no education. In 2012 the UN Committee on the Rights of the Child expressed deep concern about the centre. A BBC report in 2014 found conditions had barely improved. This is a record of institutional abuse and neglect; no sexual-abuse finding was located.
cases.cite: Greek Ombudsman report, March 2011; UN Committee on the Rights of the Child 2012; Human Rights Watch, 18 November 2014

cases.n: Serbia — 'Torment not Treatment' investigation of institutions for children and adults with disabilities
cases.place: Serbia (Kulina, Stamnica, Vršac and other institutions)
cases.who: Serbian state institutions for people with mental disabilities
cases.cover: In 2006 the director of one institution refused to let investigators see a locked area and asked them to leave; Serbian officials called the allegations 'dark propaganda'.
cases.d: Mental Disability Rights International's four-year investigation, released on 14 November 2007, covered conditions affecting more than 17,000 people with disabilities in Serbian institutions. It found children and adults tied to beds or kept in cribs for years, filthy conditions, contagious disease and no oversight, treatment it said was 'tantamount to torture'. It warned of a danger of sexual exploitation: at Vršac men and women lived in mixed wards and staff said they made no effort to determine whether sex was consensual.
cases.cite: Mental Disability Rights International, 'Torment not Treatment: Serbia's Segregation and Abuse of Children and Adults with Disabilities', November 2007

cases.n: Mogilino home for children with disabilities, Bulgaria
cases.who: Bulgarian state institution for children with physical and mental disabilities
cases.d: The BBC film 'Bulgaria's Abandoned Children' (2007, Kate Blewett) documented neglect of disabled children at the Mogilino state home. On 22 February 2008 Bulgaria's Labour and Social Policy Minister repeated a promise to close Mogilino and six similar homes, and by June 2008 children were being moved, with UNICEF working towards closure. Bulgaria has been criticised for having one of the highest numbers of children in state institutions in the EU. No sexual-abuse finding was located; this is a neglect record.
cases.cite: BBC, 'Bulgaria's Abandoned Children' (2007); Sofia Echo, 27 June 2008 (via Wikipedia)

cases.n: Colombia — ICBF investigation of 21 substitute (foster) homes
cases.place: Colombia (Soacha, Antioquia, Bogotá, Meta and other departments)
cases.victims_note: 44 children and 14 adolescents relocated from 21 foster homes under investigation.
cases.who: Instituto Colombiano de Bienestar Familiar (ICBF) substitute-home (hogar sustituto) programme
cases.d: In March 2018 the ICBF opened 21 investigations into foster homes nationwide for alleged verbal abuse, poor food and neglect and relocated 44 children and 14 adolescents, with about 3,100 homes still to review. The review followed a case in Soacha in which a man was jailed on charges of sexually abusing two girls aged 7 and 8 who were in ICBF custody in a foster home; he did not accept the charges.
cases.cite: Blu Radio, 21 March 2018 (ICBF director Karen Abudinen)

flows.n: Moldova → Russia, Turkey, Israel, UAE (trafficking of women and children, incl. institution leavers)
flows.to: Russia, Turkey, Israel, United Arab Emirates
flows.d: The US State Department (March 2007) reported women and children trafficked from Moldova for sexual exploitation, increasingly to Russia and the Middle East including Turkey, Israel and the UAE; UNICEF found children leaving Moldova's residential institutions were several times more vulnerable to trafficking than other children.
flows.cite: US State Department Human Rights Report 2006 and UNICEF 2005–2006, compiled by ACCORD query a-5839

flows.from: Orphanages and institutions across Ukraine (e.g. Vinnytsia oblast)
flows.to: Vocational schools and sex trafficking, domestic and abroad (destinations not specified)
flows.size_note: IOM: more than 120,000 Ukrainians trafficked since 1991 (all ages and routes; not only orphanage leavers). The source names no specific foreign destination, so the line ends at Kyiv.
flows.d: An IOM staff member told Disability Rights International that orphanages are a direct feeder to domestic and international human trafficking, and La Strada said recruiting children from orphanages into prostitution is 'the most typical scheme'.

flows.n: Rural Nepal (Karnali) → Kathmandu child care homes
flows.from: Karnali Province and other rural districts (e.g. Humla, Bajura, Rukum)
flows.to: Child care homes in the Kathmandu Valley
flows.d: Agents take money from rural families with promises of schooling and deliver children to Kathmandu institutions, which pay commissions; NGOs documented a forged parental death certificate used to admit a child. UNICEF estimates about 85% of children in Nepal's registered homes have a living parent or guardian.
flows.cite: The Annapurna Express, citing NCRC 2021/22 and UNICEF

flows.size_note: 549 British child migrants arrived 1948–1954 (NZ Ministry of Social Development, 2009).
flows.d: New Zealand's Social Development Minister said in November 2009 that 549 British child migrants arrived between 1948 and 1954 and that most were placed in foster care rather than institutions; IICSA lists New Zealand among the destinations of British child migration.
flows.cite: New Zealand Herald, 16 November 2009; IICSA Child Migration Programmes report, 2018

flows.n: UK → Southern Rhodesia child migrants (Rhodesia Fairbridge Memorial College)
flows.to: Rhodesia Fairbridge Memorial College, Bulawayo, Southern Rhodesia
flows.size_note: 276 children sent 1946–1956 by the Rhodesia Fairbridge Memorial Association (IICSA).
flows.d: IICSA found that children who told the headmaster they had been sexually abused by a padre at the college were beaten and warned against 'spreading malicious lies'; it lacked evidence to say whether Fairbridge UK knew of the allegations.
flows.cite: IICSA Child Migration Programmes report, 2018, section 22 (Fairbridge Society)
